title: Binance Says Hackers Used Well-Known Tricks to Carry Out a $6.34 Billion Heist
gist: Binance says North Korean-linked hackers (attributed by the FBI to TraderTraitor) stole $6.34 billion in 20 minutes on October 29 after an engineer fell for a fake job interview, then used an internal AI tool and a wallet signing service. About half was frozen; laundering is underway and could take months.

insights.claim: North Korean hackers stole $6.34 billion from Binance wallets in the biggest crypto heist to date, in about 20 minutes.
insights.speaker: Matt Burgess
insights.so_what: Largest-ever crypto theft; exchange operational security risk is material.

insights.claim: Binance says the attack began with an engineer falling for a fake job interview and downloading a malicious 'assignment', after which attackers moved through the network, exploited an internal AI tool, and reached a wallet signing service.
insights.speaker: Matt Burgess
insights.so_what: Internal AI tools can become attack paths to critical systems.
insights.quote: It was not a single isolated breach or a simple phishing incident

insights.claim: Activity traces back to June, when Engineer A downloaded a tampered Homebrew installation; in September Engineer B was recruited via a job platform and a fake video interview; attackers took control of A's and Engineer C's wallets in late October, and struck on October 29.
insights.speaker: Matt Burgess

insights.claim: The attackers abused an unauthorized internal wallet signing service to initiate transactions outside the normal withdrawal process, moving funds from hot wallets across more than 10 blockchains.
insights.speaker: Matt Burgess
insights.so_what: Controls on signing infrastructure matter more than key storage.
insights.quote: The attacker exploited unauthorized access to an internal wallet signing service

insights.claim: Binance says it has set aside funds to cover losses and has rebuilt or replaced affected internal systems, and detected and prevented 57 suspected North Korea-linked threat cases during 2026.
insights.speaker: Matt Burgess
insights.so_what: Users made whole; solvency not in question per Binance.

insights.claim: Crypto tracing firms attributed the hack to DPRK's TraderTraitor group, which previously stole over $1.5 billion in a separate hack last year, and the FBI linked it on October 31.
insights.speaker: Matt Burgess
insights.so_what: State actors dominate large crypto thefts.

insights.claim: Sophos's Rafe Pilling says TraderTraitor excels at planning and understanding victims' operations: the initial compromise is a foothold and the real attack is engineered around how the victim moves money.
insights.speaker: Rafe Pilling
insights.quote: The initial compromise is just a foothold

insights.claim: About half of the stolen funds were frozen by parts of the crypto industry, but billions remain controlled by the hackers, and cashing out could take months.
insights.speaker: Matt Burgess
insights.so_what: Stablecoin and exchange freezes partially work; residual selling risk.

insights.claim: Elliptic says laundering was highly complex and likely automated: in 3.5 days it used about 12,000 wallets across 11 blockchains, one new wallet every 25 seconds, and more than 40,000 transactions.
insights.speaker: Matt Burgess
insights.so_what: Automated cross-chain laundering stresses compliance tooling.

insights.claim: TRM Labs says North Korean-linked hackers have stolen about $12 billion in crypto since 2017, with more than half from heists this year.
insights.speaker: Matt Burgess
insights.so_what: Theft pace is accelerating sharply in 2026.

insights.claim: A report from the Multilateral Sanctions Monitoring Team says proceeds may fund North Korea's nuclear and ballistic missile programs, relying on Chinese underground banking and China-based facilitators.
insights.speaker: Matt Burgess
insights.so_what: Sanctions and secondary-sanction risk touches Chinese facilitators.
